title: Review 1 | Build the system story from data to care
overview: An integrated review of Weeks 1–6 connecting system purpose, trustworthy data, planned lifecycle, selection, interoperability, healthcare work, and HIM accountability. Use Recall → Compare → Apply → Explain to retrieve concepts, distinguish them, apply appropriate controls or system choices, and explain their role in healthcare information work.
objectives: Explain how system purpose, trustworthy data, and a planned lifecycle contribute to a reliable system.
Explain how system selection, interoperability, and data quality are connected decisions.
Apply concepts to an appropriate control, system choice, or healthcare use.
Use the Recall → Compare → Apply → Explain framework to connect concepts to healthcare information work, responsibilities, and controls.

concepts.name: Recall → Compare → Apply → Explain
concepts.definition: A review sequence: retrieve essential definitions and relationships, distinguish related concepts by purpose and function, apply concepts to a control or system choice, and connect the explanation to healthcare information work.

concepts.name: Quality, safety, and governance principles
concepts.definition: Reliable information depends on purpose and fit, data and meaning, access and trust, and workflow and adoption. Related controls include scope, workflow fit, measurable objectives, definitions, metadata, validation, mapping, policy, role-based access, authentication, logs, user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement.

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities in the integrated system
concepts.definition: Explain system purpose by identifying users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits; protect meaning through definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; protect quality by checking identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency; protect trust through privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure; and improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

concepts.name: Connected system design in healthcare
concepts.definition: A hospital connects data-quality controls, system-selection requirements, EHR architecture, and interoperability plans into one system design. Purpose, data, technology, workflow, governance, and HIM responsibility support a reliable system story.

concepts.name: High-yield comparisons
concepts.definition: The review highlights data versus information, quality versus integrity, RFI versus RFP, EMR versus EHR, internet versus intranet versus extranet, Gantt versus PERT, build versus buy versus cloud, and technical versus semantic interoperability. A useful comparison defines each term, states the difference, and gives a healthcare example.

sections.body: A reliable system begins with a clear purpose, trustworthy data, and a planned lifecycle. These are connected rather than separate concerns: the system’s purpose identifies intended users, work, outputs, and decisions; information must retain quality and meaning as it is handled; and the lifecycle organizes the work needed to create or change the system. In the integrated hospital example, data-quality controls, system-selection requirements, EHR architecture, and interoperability plans are linked as parts of one system design. For HIM, the connection matters because information quality, technology, workflow, governance, and responsibility jointly support reliable use. (Week 7 HIS.pdf [Pages 2, 5, 9])
sections.title: A connected system story

sections.body: Recall → Compare → Apply → Explain provides a practical structure for reviewing concepts. First, retrieve essential definitions and relationships. Next, compare related concepts by purpose and function rather than treating their names as interchangeable. Then apply a concept to an appropriate control or system choice. Finally, explain how it connects to healthcare information work, including what happens, who is responsible, and where control is needed. The sequence moves from knowing terms to making and explaining a relevant application. (Week 7 HIS.pdf [Page 4])
sections.title: Use the review sequence

sections.body: Four principles organize the review of quality, safety, and governance. Purpose and fit asks whether the system supports intended users, work, outputs, and decisions; scope, workflow fit, and measurable objectives are associated controls. Data and meaning concerns information that is complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood; definitions, metadata, validation, and mapping help address it. Access and trust concerns privacy, security, integrity, and auditability; policy, role-based access, authentication, and logs are listed controls. Workflow and adoption concerns whether people can use information safely and effectively; user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement support that aim. Each principle links a concern to practical evidence or control. (Week 7 HIS.pdf [Page 7])
sections.title: Controls organized by purpose

sections.body: HIM professionals connect system purpose to trustworthy information work through five responsibilities. They explain purpose by identifying users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits. They protect meaning by supporting definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation. They protect quality by checking identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency. They protect trust by supporting privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure. They improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction. Taken together, these responsibilities connect the system’s design and controls to the appropriate use of its information. (Week 7 HIS.pdf [Page 8])
sections.title: HIM accountability across the system

sections.body:
The Week 7 PDF lists eight high-yield comparison groups but does not define them or explain their differences. The distinctions below draw on the supplied prior-week ontology; the healthcare applications are illustrative applications of those concepts, not examples stated in the Week 7 PDF. (Week 7 HIS.pdf [Page 6]; supplied ontology, Weeks 1–6)

• Data vs information: Data are raw observations; information is data organized with context so it can be interpreted and used. For example, a recorded blood-pressure reading is data; that reading presented with patient and measurement context is information. (Supplied ontology: concept.data; concept.information.)

• Quality vs integrity: Data quality is fitness for use, characterized by accuracy, timeliness, completeness, consistency, accessibility, and validity. Data integrity concerns trustworthiness and preservation of meaning, supported by controls such as identity controls, audit trails, mapping, and validation. They are related but not interchangeable: quality describes fitness across dimensions, while integrity emphasizes trustworthiness and retained meaning. A hospital can check completeness and timeliness while also using identity controls and audit trails to protect integrity. (Supplied ontology: concept.data_quality; concept.data_integrity.)

• RFI vs RFP: An RFI explores the market; an RFP requests structured, comparable vendor proposals. An organization might use an RFI to understand available options, then issue an RFP so vendors respond to defined requirements in a comparable format. (Supplied ontology: concept.rfi; concept.rfp.)

• EMR vs EHR: An EMR is an electronic record within one provider or organization, focused on local clinical documentation. An EHR is a broader longitudinal record designed for authorized exchange, supporting continuity across settings and authorized users. A local clinical record and a record supporting authorized information exchange across care settings illustrate the different scopes. (Supplied ontology: concept.electronic_medical_record; concept.electronic_health_record.)

• Internet vs intranet vs extranet: The internet is a public worldwide network; an intranet is a private network for authorized employees inside one organization; an extranet is a private system that gives selected external partners controlled access. In a healthcare organization, public online services, internal employee resources, and controlled partner access illustrate the distinct access scopes. (Supplied ontology: concept.internet; concept.intranet; concept.extranet.)

• Gantt vs PERT: A Gantt chart shows when tasks start and finish and how they depend on each other; a PERT chart shows the sequence and uncertainty of activities. A project team could use a Gantt chart to view task timing and dependencies, and a PERT chart to consider activity sequence and uncertainty. (Supplied ontology: concept.gantt_chart; concept.pert_chart.)

• Build vs buy vs cloud: Build offers maximum control and tailored fit, with higher internal burden; buy offers faster access to established features, with possible workflow mismatch; cloud provides scalable, managed infrastructure and requires careful governance. These are distinct system approaches: a team weighs internal control and tailoring against speed, potential workflow fit, scalability, and governance needs when selecting an approach. (Supplied ontology: concept.build_approach; concept.buy_approach; concept.cloud_approach.)

• Technical vs semantic interoperability: The supplied ontology defines interoperability as technical connection between systems, shared meaning of information, and usable workflow presentation. Technical interoperability is the systems’ connection; semantic interoperability is the shared meaning of exchanged information. A connected exchange is not by itself enough if the receiving system or user cannot interpret the information consistently. (Supplied ontology: concept.interoperability.)

These distinctions support system and control choices by making purpose, function, scope, and trade-offs explicit. The Week 7 PDF recommends defining each term, stating the difference, and giving a healthcare example; the specific definitions above come from the supplied earlier-week ontology. (Week 7 HIS.pdf [Page 6]; supplied ontology, Weeks 1–6)
